title: Kajal Aggarwal's Next Film Calls India's Food a 'Slow Poison.' A Legal Notice Landed Before the First Poster Did.
excerpt: The India Story arrives July 24 with Shreyas Talpade, a cancer-stricken child and a courtroom showdown — and the agribusiness lobby is already lawyering up. This one's going to be a fight on and off screen.
body:
The poster tells you everything before a single ticket is sold. A father — Shreyas Talpade — cradles a cancer-stricken child in his arms, helplessness etched into every line of his face. Opposite him stands Kajal Aggarwal, jaw set, in the robes of a lawyer ready for war. Behind them looms a courthouse. And tucked into the frame, positioned exactly where an accused would stand in the dock, is a pesticide sprayer. Subtle, this film is not. Effective, it absolutely is.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Pci6yErjwt0

The India Story: Slow Poison in Progress dropped its first character poster this week, and the timing could not be more loaded. Directed by Chettan DK and written and produced by Sagar B. Shinde, the socio-political drama is set for a worldwide theatrical release on July 24, 2026, in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu. It takes aim at one of the most uncomfortable subjects in modern India — food adulteration, pesticide misuse, chemical contamination in farming, and the regulatory machinery that is supposed to stop all of it and reportedly doesn't.

And before the poster even hit timelines, the lawyers arrived.

On June 15, advocate Hiranya Pandey, acting on behalf of Bhavesh Sodha of the Agri Business Centre, served an 18-page legal notice on Zee Studios, MIG Production & Studios LLP and the film's producers. The complaint is blunt: the teaser and promotional material, it alleges, are "misleading, defamatory and scientifically unverified." It accuses the film of painting India's entire farming ecosystem as a source of "slow poison," of exaggerating pesticide usage, and of drawing an unproven line between agriculture and rising cancer rates.

The notice goes line by line. It disputes the claim that India over-uses pesticides, arguing usage per hectare is actually lower than in many countries. It objects to a suggestion that most Indian milk is adulterated. And it singles out one image in particular — a syringe being plunged into a dead chicken carcass — calling it "scientifically impossible." The complainant says the film unfairly smears millions of farmers, dairy producers and poultry businesses while spreading public fear.

Kajal, for her part, is not backing down an inch. As reports swirled about Indian mango exports facing pesticide-residue scrutiny abroad, she shared them to her stories with a pointed caption.

"This is unfortunately the story of India. This is #TheIndiaStory." — Kajal Aggarwal

It is the move of an actress who knows exactly what kind of film she signed up for — and who clearly believes in it. There is something quietly thrilling about a mainstream star planting her flag on a fight this thorny, in an industry that usually prefers its leading ladies safely apolitical.

The film itself moves beyond a single family's tragedy to indict a system — industrial negligence, corporate accountability, the slow grind of regulatory reform. The supporting cast leans into the gravity: Murali Sharma, Manish Wadhwa, Atul Tiwari and Kamlesh Sawant fill out the world, with music by Mangesh Dhakde and cinematography from Nishant Bhagwat. Presented by Zee Studios in association with MIG Production & Studios, it positions itself less as entertainment than as a national conversation-starter — the kind of issue-driven cinema that, when it lands, lands hard.

For the diaspora, this is a film with unusual pull. Food safety back home is a constant, low-grade anxiety for NRIs — the relatives who still eat from local markets, the produce you eye warily on visits, the WhatsApp forwards about adulterated paneer and chemically ripened mangoes. A courtroom drama that dramatises exactly that fear is going to find an audience from Edison to Hounslow. Expect a robust overseas theatrical run across the Hindi, Tamil and Telugu markets when it opens July 24, with a streaming window to follow.

The legal heat may yet force edits, disclaimers or a delay — these things have a way of escalating. But controversy has never hurt a film built on outrage. If anything, the agribusiness lobby has just handed The India Story the loudest free trailer money can't buy. Whether the film earns its accusations or merely exploits them, one thing is certain: this courtroom battle is going to play out twice — once on screen, and once in real life.
